title: Designing Agents (The Floor Is the Frontier) — Ben Hylak, Raindrop
talk_summary: Ben Hylak of Raindrop argues agent teams should optimize for 'raising the floor' (worst-case failures) rather than chasing benchmark ceilings, and that evals should look like code/tests rather than prompt playgrounds. He gives three tactical lessons on issue discovery: clusters are not issues, code-mode classifiers scale, and agents are bad at anomaly detection but good at investigating anomalies you've already found deterministically.

takeaways.technique: Evals as code/tests, not prompt playgrounds
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat the whole harness (prompt + tools + code) as the unit under test and write evals as unit/e2e tests in the repo (e.g. Vitest-style) rather than managed prompt-playground datasets.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the evals themselves actually should look a lot more like code. In other words, like a lot more like tests.

takeaways.technique: Track issue start-time and blast radius
takeaways.what_they_do: For every discovered defect, record when it first appeared and what fraction of runs/users it affects, so triage prioritizes new and widespread issues.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You need to know when it actually started, and you need to know how many people it affects.

takeaways.what_they_do: Don't ask agents to find anomalies; use deterministic signals (keyword frequency spikes, thresholds) to flag candidates, then have the agent investigate those specific flags.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents are very, very bad at anomaly detection. So don't ask your agent to find anomalies. Uh ask it to investigate anomalies you've already found.

takeaways.what_they_do: Write classifiers as code and run them in a sandbox at production scale over traces, rather than clustering traces or eyeballing them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: code mode actually really scales... you can write them and you can run them in a sandbox and you can run them at production scale.

takeaways.what_they_do: Prioritize eliminating worst-case failures (data deletion, wrong emails, bad recommendations) that break trust, rather than chasing emergent capability demos.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the floor is like what is the worst thing your agent can do? Like recommend a competitor or like delete a bunch of data

takeaways.what_they_do: Avoid investing months in large fixed eval sets that break whenever the model or harness changes; keep evals lightweight and adaptable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I'd be very careful about you know, uh investing you know, months in some sort of eval set that's going to you know, slow you down
